title: The elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem
one_liner: The problem every elliptic-curve scheme rests on, the square-root bound that generic attacks cannot beat, and the checks that rule out the known shortcuts.
index_meta: Primer · with the real sizes of five standard curves
description: The elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem: definition, the generic square-root bound, the curve properties that enable faster attacks and how to check for them, the largest computations on record, and Shor's algorithm.
standfirst: Given P and Q = kP, find k. For a well-chosen curve nobody knows a way to do this that is meaningfully faster than a generic collision search, and that one fact sets the size of every elliptic-curve key in use.

facts.Problem: Given P of prime order n and a point Q in the group it generates, find k with Q = kP
facts.Best known attack: Parallel Pollard rho: about √(πn/4) group operations, using the symmetry P ↔ −P
facts.Quantum: Polynomial time with Shor's algorithm; about 2,330 logical qubits estimated for P-256

blocks.p: Fix a curve E over a finite field and a point P on it whose order n is a large prime. The elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, the ECDLP, is: given a point Q in the group generated by P, find the integer k, modulo n, such that Q = kP.

On the {{c_order}}-point curve from the primer, with P = {{c_P}} and Q = {{c_kP}}, the answer is k = {{c_k}}, and a computer finds it instantly by listing multiples of P. Every elliptic-curve key pair is an instance of this problem at a size where listing is impossible: the secret key is k, the public key is kP, and the security of ECDH, ECDSA and EdDSA reduces to, or at least rests on, nobody being able to recover k.

A generic algorithm is one that uses the group only through its operations: it can add points and test them for equality, and nothing else. Shoup and, before him, Nechaev proved that any generic algorithm needs on the order of √n operations to solve the discrete logarithm problem in a group of prime order n. Baby-step giant-step meets that bound using √n memory; Pollard's rho meets it using almost none, and parallelises perfectly.

Every curve also has the symmetry P ↔ −P, which lets rho work on pairs {P, −P} and saves a factor of √2. The expected cost for a curve whose group has prime order n is then about √(πn/4) group operations. For standard curves that works out as follows.

These are the numbers behind the phrase "128-bit security": expected costs, in group operations, of recovering one key. Many keys on the same curve can be attacked for less than that each, because walks for different keys can share work: Kuhn and Struik analysed the rho method for multiple targets, and Bernstein and Lange showed how a precomputed table speeds up every later logarithm in the same group. At these sizes neither changes the conclusion, since the shared work is itself far beyond reach.

sections.heading: Curves to avoid, and how to check

blocks.p: Beating √n requires using something about the curve. Four properties are known to give attacks, and each can be checked from public data before a curve is used. The last column applies the checks to the {{c_order}}-point curve from the primer.

What it enables

Toy curve
rows: The group order has no large prime factor
Pohlig–Hellman: the problem splits into one per prime factor
The order is prime, or a large prime times a small cofactor
The MOV and Frey–Rück attacks: a pairing moves the problem into F<sub>p<sup>k</sup></sub>, where index calculus applies
The smallest k with n dividing p<sup>k</sup> − 1 is large
Smart, Satoh–Araki and Semaev: a p-adic lift solves the problem in polynomial time
A prime field, or a prime extension degree that passes the GHS test

blocks.p: The embedding-degree row shows why it is the size of the target that matters, not the existence of the map. The pairing on the toy curve does move its discrete logarithms into a finite field, but into a field of about 2<sup>{{c_emb_bits}}</sup> elements, where they are much harder than in the {{c_order}}-element group they came from. For a random curve the embedding degree is about as large as n itself. Pairing-based cryptography deliberately uses curves with small embedding degree, and sizes them so that the field side is hard too.

blocks.note: A strong curve can still be used insecurely. An implementation that accepts a point without checking that it lies on the curve can be fed a point of small order on a different curve, and will leak the secret key a few bits at a time. The curve's twist, which such points often land on, should be secure as well. These are implementation checks rather than properties of the ECDLP, and the Pohlig–Hellman page covers them. SafeCurves collects all of these criteria and applies them to published curves.

blocks.p: The largest discrete logarithms computed in public on elliptic curves are far from cryptographic sizes. The prime-field record is 114 bits, set in 2017 by Kusaka and collaborators on a Barreto–Naehrig curve, with about 2,000 CPU cores over six months. Before that, Bos, Kaihara, Kleinjung, Lenstra and Montgomery solved the 112-bit standard curve secp112r1 in 2009 on a cluster of PlayStation 3 consoles. On binary curves, the 113-bit standard curves sect113r1 and sect113r2 were solved on FPGA clusters in 2015 and 2016.

The next public target is Certicom's ECC2K-130, a Koblitz curve over F2131 with a subgroup of about 2129 points, whose expected cost Bailey and collaborators put at 260.9 iterations. It has been open since 1997, and we are running a distributed attack on it. The distance from there to a 256-bit curve is a factor of about 267 in work.

For the multiplicative group of a finite field, index calculus gives subexponential attacks, and whether anything like it works on elliptic curves has been studied for decades. Over extension fields it does: Gaudry and Diem, building on Semaev's summation polynomials, gave algorithms that beat rho for curves over F<sub>q<sup>n</sup></sub>. Over prime fields nobody has found a factor base that yields relations cheaply enough, and no published attack on a prime-field curve improves on generic methods.

Index calculus, end to end runs both the classical algorithm and Gaudry's elliptic version on small examples, and the explainer on three settings compares prime fields, characteristic 2 and Koblitz curves.

Shor's algorithm solves discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer, and elliptic curves are no exception. Roetteler, Naehrig, Svore and Lauter estimated that a curve over an n-bit prime field needs at most 9n + 2⌈log<sub>2</sub> n⌉ + 10 logical qubits: 2,330 for P-256, with about 1.26 × 10<sup>11</sup> Toffoli gates. The same paper puts factoring a 3072-bit RSA modulus at 6,146 logical qubits, so the elliptic-curve key falls to a smaller machine than an RSA key of similar classical strength.

No quantum computer of that size exists. The concern is that data encrypted today with elliptic-curve key exchange can be recorded now and decrypted once one does, which is why key exchange is moving first: see ML-KEM, and for signatures ML-DSA.
